summary: Researchers found that the authenticated encryption in the original SSH transport protocol is vulnerable to several attacks. This document describes new symmetric encryption methods for SSH and gives specific recommendations on how often implementations should rekey. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: Someone found a weak spot in how a secret-message lock worked. This adds sturdier locks and says to swap the keys often.

subtitle: New counter-mode ciphers for SSH, plus firm advice on how often to swap encryption keys.

tldr.problem: Researchers found that the CBC-based encryption in the original SSH Transport Protocol is open to a chosen-plaintext privacy attack, and that too little rekeying can leak information about payload data whatever the cipher.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds thirteen encryption methods that run a block cipher in stateful-decryption counter (SDCTR) mode, and sets limits on how many packets and blocks may be sent before rekeying.
tldr.outcome: The counter-mode methods are the preferred replacement for the CBC methods in RFC 4253, and the rekeying limits tighten that RFC's one-gigabyte suggestion.

facts.label: Block rekey limit
facts.value: 2**(L/4) blocks when L is at least 128

today: RFC 4344 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It tells implementers to treat the counter-mode methods as the preferred alternatives to the insecure CBC methods in RFC 4253.

sections.title: Why SSH Encryption Needed Fixing
sections.content:
The symmetric part of the SSH Transport Protocol, defined in RFC 4253, was meant to give both privacy and integrity for the data it carries. Researchers found several security problems with it. The encryption mode in RFC 4253 is open to a chosen-plaintext privacy attack. Separately, if keys are not replaced often enough, the protocol may leak information about payload data, and that is true whatever encryption mode is used.

The same researchers showed how to modify the symmetric part so that it provably keeps privacy and integrity against chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext and reaction attacks. This RFC turns those recommendations into concrete encryption methods and rekeying advice. It uses the data types of RFC 4251 and the transport protocol of RFC 4253.
sections.eli5: People found that the old lock on SSH could be tricked in some clever ways. This document hands out a better lock and tells you how often to change the key.

sections.title: The Two Rekeying Recommendations
sections.content:
RFC 4253 suggests rekeying after every gigabyte of transmitted data. This RFC gives firmer upper bounds, as two recommendations. The first protects against leakage through the MAC tag, the second against leakage through the block cipher.

First recommendation. After a key exchange, an implementation SHOULD NOT send more than 232 packets before rekeying again. It SHOULD also try to rekey before receiving more than 232 packets, and the preferred way is to rekey after receiving more than 231 packets.

Second recommendation. Let L be the cipher's block length in bits (128 for AES). If L is at least 128, an implementation SHOULD NOT encrypt more than 2L/4 blocks with one key, and should also try to force a rekey before receiving more than that. If L is below 128, as with 3DES, Blowfish, CAST-128 and IDEA, it is still advisable to follow RFC 4253 and rekey at least once per gigabyte.

Depending on the block length and packet sizes, either recommendation can be the stricter one. If L is 128 or less, the second supersedes the first.
sections.eli5: A key is like a tool that wears out the more you use it. The rules say to swap it for a fresh one after a set amount of use, so nobody has enough clues to guess your secrets.

sections.title: Stateful-Decryption Counter Mode
sections.content:
In stateful-decryption counter mode (SDCTR), the sender and receiver each keep an internal L-bit counter X. Its starting value is the initial IV from RFC 4253, read as an unsigned integer in network byte order. When X reaches (2L)-1, incrementing it sets it back to 0.

To encrypt a packet, split it into blocks of L bits. Encrypt the counter with the cipher to get a block, XOR that block with the first plaintext block to make the first ciphertext block, then increment the counter and repeat. Decryption does the same thing: encrypt the counter, XOR with the ciphertext. The counter itself is never sent. Because the keystream can be precomputed, both encryption and decryption are parallelizable.

The existing rules still hold. Each direction runs independently, and the packet length, padding length, payload and padding fields MUST be encrypted, with their combined length a multiple of the cipher's block size.
sections.eli5: Imagine a secret code machine that turns a counter, one, two, three, into scrambled noise. You mix that noise into your message. The other side runs the same counter and mixes the noise back out.

sections.title: The Thirteen New Methods
sections.content:
The RFC defines thirteen methods named <cipher>-ctr, in addition to the ones in Section 6.3 of RFC 4253. Four are RECOMMENDED: aes128-ctr, aes192-ctr, aes256-ctr and 3des-ctr. The others are OPTIONAL and use Blowfish, Twofish, Serpent, IDEA or CAST-128.

Details differ by cipher. 3des-ctr uses three-key triple-DES and needs 24 bytes of key data, of which 168 bits are used. blowfish-ctr uses 256-bit keys, whereas blowfish-cbc from RFC 4253 uses 128-bit keys. AES, Twofish and Serpent have a 16-byte block; 3DES, Blowfish, IDEA and CAST-128 have an 8-byte block.

The RFC says a future specification will likely promote aes128-ctr to REQUIRED, and that implementing it is very strongly encouraged.
sections.eli5: It is a menu of thirteen lock styles. A few are marked as the ones you really should have, and the rest are extras you can pick if you like.

sections.title: Security Reasoning
sections.content:
The research papers prove that an SSH application using these methods and recommendations resists a large class of privacy and integrity attacks. The RFC explains this is a reductionist proof: an attacker who breaks the SSH symmetric layer would also break an underlying piece such as the block cipher or the MAC. Attacks are not impossible, only extremely improbable if building blocks like AES are secure. Developers must still take care, for example not to store keys in cleartext in an unprotected file.

On the first rekeying limit: past 232 packets under one key, replay and re-ordering attacks become possible, and the MAC may leak payload information. An attacker looks for a collision between MACs of two packets that used the same 32-bit sequence number; a collision probably means identical payloads. Compression and random padding reduce but do not remove the risk. The RFC does not lengthen the sequence number because that could hurt interoperability with older SSH versions.

On the second limit: counter mode has a theoretical privacy attack if an attacker can get about 2L/2 messages encrypted with one key, and encrypting more than 2L blocks would reuse keystream. Counter mode needs no random padding, which saves generating random bytes per packet. Padding must still be a multiple of the block length, so the packet format of RFC 4253 is unchanged and exact payload length is not revealed.
sections.eli5: Mathematicians showed the new locks are only breakable if the basic building blocks are broken first. They also warn that using one key for too long gives sneaky people too many clues.

sections.title: IANA Registry Entries
sections.content: The thirteen encryption algorithm names from the encryption methods section were added to the Secure Shell Encryption Algorithm Name registry established by Section 4.11.1 of RFC 4250. That registry is how implementations agree on a name when they negotiate which cipher to use.
sections.eli5: The new lock names were written in the official list of SSH lock names, so everyone spells them the same way.
